promptText: Why is naively asking a model to 'return JSON' and parsing with ObjectMapper.readValue() considered fragile in production?
options: ObjectMapper cannot parse JSON produced by LLMs under any circumstances
The model may add explanatory preamble text, wrap the JSON in a markdown fence, or produce minor syntax issues like trailing commas, intermittently breaking a naive parser
JSON is not a supported response format for any LLM provider
ObjectMapper requires the response to be gzip-compressed
explanation: A plain natural-language request is a soft instruction the model can deviate from -- adding a preamble, a code fence, or invalid syntax -- causing an intermittent, hard-to-triage JsonParseException in production.

promptText: What is the key structural difference between BeanOutputConverter<T>, MapOutputConverter, and ListOutputConverter in Spring AI?
options: They differ only in performance, not in target type
BeanOutputConverter targets a specific POJO/record via a derived JSON Schema; MapOutputConverter targets a generic Map<String,Object>; ListOutputConverter targets a flat List<String>
MapOutputConverter is deprecated in favor of BeanOutputConverter
ListOutputConverter is the only one that supports nested objects
explanation: Each converter targets a different output shape: a typed DTO via reflection-derived schema, a loosely-typed map for exploratory extraction, or a flat list for simple enumerations like tags.

promptText: Why can't you write entity(List<Order>.class) in Spring AI, and what's the correct alternative?
options: List<Order>.class is valid syntax, but it's simply slower than the alternative
Java erases generic type parameters at runtime, so List<Order>.class isn't legal; instead, pass a ParameterizedTypeReference<List<Order>> that captures the full generic signature
Spring AI only supports arrays, never List types, for structured output
You must manually write a custom Jackson deserializer for every generic type
explanation: Generic type erasure means the JVM only ever sees List.class; ParameterizedTypeReference captures the full generic signature in its own class hierarchy so the target type isn't lost at runtime.

promptText: Under prompt-injected schema enforcement (Path A), what happens at each generation step to keep the model's output on-schema?
options: The inference engine masks out any token that would make the output invalid, guaranteeing conformance
Nothing at the decoding layer prevents deviation -- the model is simply given natural-language instructions describing the desired schema and remains free to ignore them
The model automatically retries itself until valid JSON is produced
Spring AI intercepts and rewrites invalid tokens in real time as they're generated
explanation: Path A appends the schema as text instructions to the prompt; the model generates tokens with nothing at the decoding layer enforcing compliance, making this a soft, non-guaranteed constraint.

promptText: Which annotation would you add to a POJO field to give the model additional semantic guidance about an ambiguous field like severity, beyond just its type?
options: @NotNull
@JsonPropertyDescription
@Component
@Transactional
explanation: @JsonPropertyDescription compiles into the generated JSON Schema's description field, giving the model semantic context that a bare field name and type cannot convey.

promptText: Even under a provider's strongest native 'structured outputs' guarantee (constrained/grammar-based decoding), what can still go wrong that structural enforcement alone cannot catch?
options: The output can still be syntactically invalid JSON
The output can be perfectly schema-conformant in shape and type, yet semantically wrong (e.g., an incorrect enum value or an implausible number)
The response will always be missing required fields
Nothing -- native structured output eliminates all possible failure modes
explanation: Constrained decoding guarantees syntactic and structural conformance, never semantic conformance -- a schema-valid object can still contain a confidently wrong value, which only downstream validation can catch.

promptText: Mechanically, what does provider-native constrained decoding do differently from prompt-injected schema instructions to enforce structure?
options: It runs a second LLM call afterward to fix any malformed JSON

At every decoding step, it masks out (zeroes the probability of) any token that would make the output unable to complete into a valid instance of the schema, so the model can only sample from schema-legal tokens
It converts the model's raw text output into JSON using a client-side regex after generation
It requires the developer to manually validate each token as it streams in
explanation: Constrained decoding compiles the schema into a constraint automaton and masks illegal tokens at each step before sampling, guaranteeing the final string is syntactically valid and schema-conformant by construction.

promptText: Why is tool/function calling described in this chapter as an early 'backdoor' for achieving structured output?
options: Because tool calling and structured output use completely unrelated infrastructure that happened to converge by coincidence

Because defining a fake 'function' whose parameters match your desired schema and forcing the model to call it leverages the provider's tool-calling machinery -- often trained/constrained more rigorously than plain text generation -- to get schema-conformant output before providers offered a dedicated response-format feature
Because tool calling bypasses billing for the underlying model call
Because it was the only method that worked before JSON existed as a data format
explanation: Because a malformed function call is unambiguously useless, providers trained and constrained tool-calling more rigorously, so repurposing it purely for structured extraction became a reliable stopgap before native response formats existed.

promptText: A teammate wants to remove all downstream Bean Validation now that structured output 'works' and returns a well-formed object every time. What's the flaw in this plan?
options: Bean Validation is required by Spring AI internally and cannot be removed regardless
Structural conformance (valid shape/types) says nothing about whether the field values are semantically or factually correct -- a confidently wrong value can still be perfectly schema-valid
BeanOutputConverter automatically performs all necessary business-rule validation already
Removing Bean Validation would break JSON deserialization entirely
explanation: Structural conformance and correctness are distinct problems; even a strong constrained-decoding guarantee never checks whether the values themselves are semantically valid, which is exactly what Bean Validation is for.

promptText: In a production retry/repair loop for structured output failures, why is feeding the specific parse or validation error back into the re-prompt more effective than a generic 'please try again' instruction?
options: It isn't more effective -- generic retries and specific retries have statistically identical recovery rates
Specific corrective feedback (e.g., naming the exact invalid enum value) gives the model concrete information about what went wrong, which measurably improves the odds of a corrected response
Specific feedback is required because Spring AI rejects generic retry prompts at the API level
It reduces token cost, which is the only reason it's preferred
explanation: A retry that tells the model precisely what was wrong recovers more often than a generic retry, because it gives the model actionable information rather than asking it to guess what needs correcting.

promptText: Why should schema descriptions or field names injected into a structured-output prompt never be built directly from unsanitized user input?
options: Spring AI's schema generator will throw a compile-time error if user input is detected

An attacker-controlled schema description could smuggle instruction-like text into what the model treats as system guidance -- the same prompt-injection risk as any other untrusted text reaching the model
User input cannot be serialized into valid JSON Schema syntax under any circumstances
It would violate Jackson's naming convention rules and cause deserialization to fail
explanation: Assembling structural instructions from unsanitized user text is a prompt-injection surface; the mitigation is keeping the schema itself developer-defined and static, treating only the extracted data as user-controlled.

promptText: Why does the chapter argue that structural validity and semantic correctness must be treated as two entirely distinct failure classes when designing a retry strategy, rather than handling both with the same generic re-prompt?
options: They aren't actually distinct -- any retry strategy that fixes one automatically fixes the other

A structural failure (invalid JSON/shape) is often recoverable by a formatting-focused reprompt or even a cheaper model, while a semantic failure (valid shape, wrong values) usually isn't fixable by simply re-asking and often signals the task needs better grounding or isn't a good fit for the model
Structural failures can only be fixed by upgrading the model version, never by retrying
Semantic failures always resolve themselves automatically on the second attempt
explanation: Conflating structural and semantic failures is a common mistake senior interviews probe for: a formatting slip is fixable by a precision-focused reprompt, while a wrong-but-well-shaped value usually indicates a deeper task or grounding problem.

promptText: For a service with a strict p99 latency budget that occasionally hits structured-output parse failures, what design choice specifically protects the latency SLA while still attempting recovery?
options: Retry indefinitely until a valid response is produced, since correctness matters more than latency

Cap retries to a small bounded number (e.g., 1-2), optionally routing the repair attempt to a faster/cheaper model since precision rather than creativity is what's needed, and fail to an explicit fallback if retries are exhausted
Disable structured output entirely and switch to unstructured prose to avoid parse failures
Increase the model's temperature on retry to encourage a more creative correction
explanation: Every retry is a full additional model call that threatens a p99 budget; a bounded retry count with a fast repair model and an explicit fallback path protects the SLA while still giving the failure a chance to recover.

promptText: A platform team is building a single internal API so every team can request structured output from any LLM provider. What is one thing this abstraction must deliberately NOT hide from callers, and why?
options: The exact wording of the injected JSON Schema instructions, because teams need to memorize it for debugging

Whether a given provider/model combination is actually providing a soft (prompt-injected) or hard (decode-constrained) enforcement guarantee -- silently normalizing this away would let teams build false confidence into SLAs that a quiet provider downgrade could later violate undetected
The specific HTTP status codes returned by each provider's API
The internal Java package structure of the abstraction's implementation classes
explanation: Hiding which enforcement level a provider actually gives would let teams build false confidence into SLAs and incident runbooks, and make a provider migration that quietly downgrades guarantees invisible until it causes an incident.

promptText: Why does the chapter recommend batching a 50-item classification task into one call returning List<Classification> rather than issuing 50 separate structured-output calls, and what's the trade-off?
options: Batching is always strictly better with no downside -- there's no real trade-off

One batched call is dramatically cheaper and faster in aggregate than 50 separate calls, at the cost of slightly higher per-call complexity and a higher blast radius if that single call fails structurally
Spring AI technically forbids making more than one structured-output call per HTTP request
Batching is only relevant for streaming responses, not structured output
explanation: Batch extraction beats per-item calls where the schema allows it, but concentrates risk: a single structural failure in one large batched response affects all 50 items at once rather than just one.
